newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania sacks doctors after sick man left to die.
newsitem.headline: Romania sacks doctors after sick man left to die.

text.p: Romanian health authorities sacked three doctors and ordered an inquiry on Thursday after a man diagnosed with tuberculosis was denied entry to three hospitals and was left by an ambulance to die on the street.

"The doctors who refused to admit this sick man bear the same guilt as the ambulance nurse who abandoned him," Alexandru Ciocilteu, head of the Bucharest health department, told journalists after an emergency meeting.
Romanian television showed the body of the 41-year-old man, wearing only pyjama bottoms and with a intravenous drip in his arm, lying on a pavement.

Investigations found that three Bucharest hospitals refused to admit him on Wednesday because he did not live in the appropriate city district. The ambulance nurse left him at the address on his identity papers and he was found dead in the morning.
An initial inquiry prompted the dismissal of doctors responsible for admissions at the three hospitals. The nurse was put under investigation for manslaughter.
Doctors, top politicians and the media said the case exposed deep flaws in an underfunded medical system and cast doubt on moral values seven years after the fall of communism.
"Government officials responsible for the institutions involved in this scandal will be called to account," said Petre Roman, chairman of the upper house of parliament, the Senate.
"I fear the blame will be laid only on the ambulance workers. But the issue is much wider and things cannot stop there. We know that something is rotten in this system."

Romania's health care system degenerated during 50 years of communism despite lofty pledges of free medicine for all. Some hospitals have still not recovered from the 1977 earthquake which destroyed much of Bucharest.
Since 1989, health care has virtually collapsed under bad management, misuse of funds, lack of medicines and equipment, underpaid staff and overcrowded and filthy hospitals.

Poverty, malnutrition and poor hygiene have reduced life expectancy and led to a comeback of such illnesses as viral meningitis, typhoid and cholera. Tuberculosis and veneral diseases are on the rise and the country is afflicted by 54 percent of Europe's juvenile AIDS cases.

The newly-elected centrist government is championing a health insurance bill setting up Western-style social security contributions. It also intends to boost morale among doctors, who now earn less than $70 per month, by linking pay to the number of patients treated.
